subsubtopic: USE OF SIN-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity, to move as follows:
That this House calls on the government to set aside, as bureaucratic "snoopery" which interferes with the civil rights and privacy of Canadians, the regulations under law under which social insurance numbers must be produced, failing which 25 per cent of the interest on bonds is held back and the sale and purchases of stock without such a number is denied.

subsubtopic: MOVEMENT OF GRAIN-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Since the movement of grain out of Manitoba has almost stopped and, according to sources in the grain industry, the province of Manitoba will not see any significant movement of grain until January, 1979, at the earliest, I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie):
That Canadian grain cars be recalled immediately from the United States and pressed into service, moving barley and lower grades of wheat out of the province of Manitoba so that Manitoba farmers will have some available cash with which to pay their bills.

subtopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF FIRST DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER OF ROMANIA

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF FIRST DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER OF ROMANIA
speechtext: Before proceeding with the question period, I call attention to the presence in our gallery of a distinguished visitor, in the person of the First Deputy Prime Minister of Romania, Mr. Gheroghe Oprea.

subtopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF FIRST DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER OF ROMANIA
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: RATE OF INFLATION-LEVEL OF UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Finance, who is just coming into the House. As the Prime Minister, in Toronto over the weekend, told Ontario Liberals that we in the opposition and the media were his enemy in that we are too critical, would the Minister of Finance tell the House how we can put a better slant on our current 8.2 per cent inflation, bearing in mind that inflation was about 4 per cent when the Prime Minister first took power, which is well up from the 2 per cent average prior to his gaining power in this country?

subsubtopic: RATE OF INFLATION-LEVEL OF UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, first I should like to tell the hon. member that indeed I was in the House. Since he saw me circulating, I do not know why he took the occasion to tell them on television that I was not in my seat.

subsubtopic: RATE OF INFLATION-LEVEL OF UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: RATE OF INFLATION-LEVEL OF UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: I was here at two o'clock. I think the hon. member is not seeking information; he is just trying to make some political points.

subsubtopic: RATE OF INFLATION-LEVEL OF UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: RATE OF INFLATION-LEVEL OF UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, again my question is directed to the Minister of Finance, who must slip around so quietly that certainly I did not perceive he was in the House earlier.

subsubtopic: RATE OF INFLATION-LEVEL OF UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: RATE OF INFLATION-LEVEL OF UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
My follow-up question to the Minister of Finance deals with unemployment. Could he tell us how we should interpret the present unemployment level in Canada of
8.2	per cent, bearing in mind that when the Prime Minister took power it was a mere 4 per cent? I ask this question in the context of the Prime Minister's suggestion that we are a little too critical, judging from his remarks in Toronto.

subsubtopic: RATE OF INFLATION-LEVEL OF UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, he said that opposition members were a little bit too critical because the financial critics of the opposition never mentioned that we have created 2.3 million new jobs in Canada in the last seven years.

subsubtopic: RATE OF INFLATION-LEVEL OF UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: RATE OF INFLATION-LEVEL OF UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my final supplementary is directed to the Minister of Finance. In due course, I hope he will try to explain his answer to the 900,000 people who are still out of work in this country.

subsubtopic: RATE OF INFLATION-LEVEL OF UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Plus the hidden jobless.

subsubtopic: RATE OF INFLATION-LEVEL OF UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Since Canada, for four years in a row, has been the only industrial nation to run a current account world deficit, would the minister tell the House in what way this has been good for Canada, bearing in mind that while we likely will lose $4 billion to $5 billion internationally this year, Italy, France, Britain, West Germany and Japan all will run substantial surpluses in their current positions with the rest of the world?

subsubtopic: RATE OF INFLATION-LEVEL OF UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is asking me to compare the economy of Germany or France with that of Canada, a country which must develop its monumental resources year after year in order to boost its economy from coast to coast and from Windsor to the North Pole, which is very difficult to do. Obviously, over the years, Canadians have been obliged to borrow capital to develop their vast country and that is why we now have current account deficits. But I want to mention that among all western hemisphere countries, Canada is the one which has the largest per capita trade surplus.
November 20, 1978

subtopic: MARITIMES-EFFECT ON ECONOMY OF HIGH INTEREST RATES

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subtopic: MARITIMES-EFFECT ON ECONOMY OF HIGH INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, can the minister explain, or perhaps tell the House what steps, other than those announced in the budget, he intends to take to offset the 10.75 per cent increase in the prime rate in the slow growth regions of the country, especially in the five eastern provinces which already account for over half the total unemployment in the country, and on which provinces this high interest rate will slow growth considerably more?

subtopic: MARITIMES-EFFECT ON ECONOMY OF HIGH INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have put many more resources at the disposal of the Minister of Employment and Immigration for his program this winter to cope with the problems of unemployment. In turn, particularly to help the maritime provinces in developing and having more investment, we have doubled from 10 to 20 the investment tax credit. We have done the same for research and development. This is the first time, since I became the Minister of Finance, that we have found enough flexibility in our policies to have fiscal policies which are conducive to more growth in the maritimes and the rest of Canada, and to have a special fiscal policy for the maritimes.

subtopic: MARITIMES-EFFECT ON ECONOMY OF HIGH INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MARITIMES-EFFECT ON ECONOMY OF HIGH INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister is attempting to salvage what is left of his reputation as Minister of Finance, and the Prime Minister is attempting to explain away ten years of mismanagement by the government. According to the 1977 figures of Statistics Canada, especially in the Atlantic provinces and Quebec, family incomes have fallen behind by
4.5	per cent in real terms, thereby adding another 300,000 Canadians to the list of those already below the poverty line. Since this is something the minister cannot be proud of, perhaps he can explain why it is so. Let him explain that away.

subtopic: MARITIMES-EFFECT ON ECONOMY OF HIGH INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the night of the budget I explained that in the last three years Canadians have increased their net income by 7 per cent while our southern neighbours have seen their net income go down by 2 per cent. I think that is a performance we should be proud of.

subtopic: MARITIMES-EFFECT ON ECONOMY OF HIGH INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, keeping in mind the slow growth rate of the country and the government's pitiful record in regional development, perhaps the minister and his colleague, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, will look at what has been happening in the New England states adjacent to the Atlantic provinces, particularly at their growth rates and their rates of unemployment-which are the envy of the country-to determine what they are doing right and what this government is doing wrong. Has the minister examined that?
Oral Questions CONSUMER AFFAIRS

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. This morning, Ken Crawford, president of the Canadian Turkey Marketing Agency, said that wholesalers in the turkey business in Canada are withholding some 50 million pounds of turkeys from the market on an artificial basis in order to drive up prices before Christmas. He also predicted that if the government does not force them to release these 50 million pounds of turkeys, the price paid by Canadians will be the highest we have experienced in the last 45 years.
I would ask the minister whether he is aware of that situation and, if so, what is he doing to prevent the wholesalers from driving up prices artificially?

speakeroldname: Hon. Warren Allmand (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, I was not aware of that. As a matter of fact, during the summer and on several occasions since, I have made public statements urging marketing boards to increase the production of turkeys as an alternative to beef with such high prices. I have taken an opposite approach, and I am certainly surprised by this particular set of events.

Mr. Speaker, the marketing board says we have 50 million pounds of turkeys artificially being held back by the wholesalers, not the marketing board, with another 50 million pounds of turkeys now in the process of being killed and put on stream, which is about half the turkey production in this country. So the turkeys are there.
Since the farm price for turkeys went up by four cents a pound, and according to a government study in August the consumer price has gone up by some 15 cents a pound, I would ask the minister whether he has considered referring this matter to the combines investigations branch to determine whether this comes under consumer gouging or price fixing by the turkey wholesalers of this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am alarmed by the allegations of the hon. member, and I certainly will pursue the matter.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the minister will soon receive in his office the press statement by the turkey marketing agency of Canada, and from the president who held a press conference this morning, saying the things I am now saying in the House, namely, that as a result of this artificial stockpiling by the wholesalers, the retailers have now gone to the Canadian turkey marketing agency asking it to press for a further importation of turkeys from the United States to the tune of some three million pounds.
I would like to ask the minister whether he can assure us he will recommend to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce that the supplementary import permit be denied and that, instead, he will force the turkey wholesalers to put on stream these turkeys they are holding back in order that we can have more jobs in Canadian agriculture and processing.

November 20, 1978
Oral Questions

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will be glad to pursue the recommendations made by the hon. member, but I want to check the facts first.

subsubtopic: THE BUDGET-ECONOMIC GROWTH
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want to direct a question to the Minister of Finance. Now that he has admitted real growth in the country will be around, or less than, 4 per cent this year, yet only 13 months ago he was saying we must have growth of at least 5 per cent or 6 per cent if we are to bring unemployment right down, I would ask the minister whether the government is giving up the proposition that one of the functions of budget-making, and one of the functions of economic policy-making, is to create reasonably full employment in the country.

subsubtopic: THE BUDGET-ECONOMIC GROWTH
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is always the objective of the government to create as much employment as possible and to review the level of unemployment. At the same time, we have to set our policies against the flexibility we have in present circumstances. Of course, we have had 4 per cent growth, or close to it, rather than 5 per cent as expected. There is less growth in all OECD nations than predicted. Even with a growth of 4 per cent, as I said, we managed in the last year to create 368,000 new jobs, while with 5 per cent growth last year we predicted we were going to have less than 300,000 jobs. So under the circumstances I think we have done quite well in terms of employment over the last 12 months.

subsubtopic: THE BUDGET-ECONOMIC GROWTH
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I am always astonished when the Minister of Finance quotes figures for growth of jobs. That is totally irrelevant; the question is how many people are out of work and what is the unemployment rate. That is what is important. It is also clear from the budget that the minister was not really making any really concerted attack on inflation. Given the fact that for the last 40 years the goal of budget-making has been to have relatively full employment and reasonable price stability, I am trying to discover, through my questions to the minister today, what were the goals of this particular budget, which is doing nothing about unemployment and nothing about inflation. What was the Minister of Finance trying to achieve in this budget?

subsubtopic: THE BUDGET-ECONOMIC GROWTH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, through the different measures that we have put forward, we have reduced income taxes paid by workers in Canada by almost $2 billion. We have also helped, thereby, to put more money in the hands of the people to buy more goods next year. We have also reduced the sales tax in order to reduce the cost of those goods which Canadians will be buying. At the same time as doing all that, we have managed to reduce the cash requirements of the government,

because in the month of August we were able to produce some cuts in expenditures.
The policy of the government is to make more money available in the hands of the workers, and to lower prices. In doing so, we will be more competitive and, in being more competitive, we will have more people working in Canada's labour force.

subsubtopic: THE BUDGET-ECONOMIC GROWTH
speechtext: A final supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I come back to the Minister of Finance because I think this is an important point. One has to be pragmatic and take into consideration what the minister has provided in his budget. Under the budget, neither unemployment nor inflation will be substantially reduced in this nation. Am I correct in understanding that the minister has said today that the principal goal of this budget was to reduce the cash requirements of the government? Is that the major aim of budget-making in Canada at the present time?

subsubtopic: THE BUDGET-ECONOMIC GROWTH
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have just clearly indicated that the purpose of this budget was to control the level of inflation which has varied this year between 816 per cent and 9 per cent. We hope that this level will be reduced next year to 616 per cent. We hope also to create next year some 250,000 additional new jobs, which indicates that we are very concerned about the level of employment in Canada, and we have succeeded in introducing such a budget while reducing the cash flow requirements from $12 billion to $10.7 billion.

speakeroldname: Mr. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Acting Prime Minister. Between 1970 and 1976, Canada's share of the world market for manufactured exports fell from 6 per cent to 4.7 per cent. At the same time, the world demand for manufactured exports was increasing at an amazing rate.
I would ask the Acting Prime Minister, does he agree with the analysis of the Science Council of Canada's, Mr. John Shepherd and Mr. John Orr-this being a government appointed agency, by the way-that the real weakness in Canadian industry is in the area of fully manufactured goods? If the Acting Prime Minister agrees with that, what steps is he going to take to overcome this weakness, or does he think that these statements are balderdash?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and President of Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, I do not believe that these statements are balderdash, even though when repeated by the hon. member they have not improved in transmission. They are serious views which will be taken into account by the government in its ongoing effort to develop and implement an industrial policy in Canada.

A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I am glad the Acting Prime Minister does not believe that these

November 20, 1978
statements are balderdash. Could he explain to the House why the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce has said that the Science Council experts are talking balderdash, as reported on November 13 in the Montreal Gazette and in every other newspaper that carries Canadian Press reports? The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce has said that they are talking balderdash, and I quote him: he said, "What do they know about running a business or the real business world?" Who speaks for the government in this matter, the minister, who spouts balderdash, or the Acting Prime Minister who has just answered my question?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would not conclude that the use of the word "balderdash" is a matter of government policy. I hope it does not become a matter of great concern in the Conservative caucus.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. Some ten days ago I asked him about a pending government decision with regard to the public utilities tax refunding act. He indicated it would be decided at that week's cabinet meeting. Is the minister now in a position to tell the House whether there has been a decision? Has it been indicated to the ministers of finance of the provinces, and is he prepared to tell the House what the government is prepared to do about this question?
Mr. Speaker, I am not in a position today to report anything new to the House.

A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Could the hon. minister tell me whether he has the concurrence of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce in regard to this policy as enunciated by the President of the Treasury Board, since this proposal mostly affects the province of Alberta in a very negative way?

Mr. Speaker, I just said that when the time comes, I will report to the House of Commons. Discussions within cabinet are not for public exposure. I am going along very well with the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce.
Balderdash!

subsubtopic: RCMP INVESTIGATION OF BOEING CONTRACT-REQUEST FOR PROGRESS REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Solicitor General. It is now more than 18 months since the first published reports that Boeing was making so-called dual contract payments to its agents in Canada.
Oral Questions
Will the minister tell the House approximately when the RCMP investigation was begun, whether there has been an interim or progress report since then to a minister or ministers and, for the record, when does he expect the final report?

subsubtopic: RCMP INVESTIGATION OF BOEING CONTRACT-REQUEST FOR PROGRESS REPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the matter was raised by me on a number of occasions with the RCMP. In reply to the hon. gentleman's question, I can only indicate to him that, as has been the practice in the past, the investigation is ongoing. I cannot advise the hon. gentleman at this time when it will be concluded, but I can indicate to him that I will be pleased to report to the House any progress in the matter.

subsubtopic: RCMP INVESTIGATION OF BOEING CONTRACT-REQUEST FOR PROGRESS REPORT
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. The minister neglected to mention that I was told by the government a month ago that if I would be patient I would soon be satisfied one way or another with an answer. As Boeing stated that they executed dual consulting agreements in connection with sales in Canada, it would seem logical for the inquiry into this matter to start with the individual or company most likely to know the practice of Boeing during dual consulting agreements, that is, the regular consultant for Boeing in Canada. Has this been done? Can the minister tell me that and, if not, will he undertake to find out and report back to the House?

subsubtopic: RCMP INVESTIGATION OF BOEING CONTRACT-REQUEST FOR PROGRESS REPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the question the hon. gentleman poses requests information that would reveal the nature of the investigation and the progress of that investigation, which is something which I am not at liberty to do. In terms of the undertaking that he wishes me to give, I cannot give it.

subsubtopic: DISPOSABLE INCOME FOR CANADIAN EMPLOYEES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question arising from an earlier question to the Minister of Finance. Could the minister inform the House how he can talk in his budget and, again, in answers given today, about the need for a greater competitive position between Canada and the United States and at the same time stress the fact that real disposable income for employees in Canada has risen in real terms by 7 per cent, while it has declined in the United States by 2 per cent? It seems to me those two statements are in direct conflict and I should like the minister to explain.

subsubtopic: DISPOSABLE INCOME FOR CANADIAN EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I suggest there is nothing wrong in saying that the situation of Canadian workers has improved over the past three years. We must see to it that the competitive position between Canada and the United States does not deteriorate in the future because of excessive increases in wages and prices. One does not contradict oneself when one says to Canadian employees

November 20, 1978
Oral Questions
that they have improved their situation over the past three years and that they must limit their demands in the future to help Canada maintain its current competitive position with the United States.

subsubtopic: DISPOSABLE INCOME FOR CANADIAN EMPLOYEES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, can the Minister of Finance tell us, at this time, whether or not the disposable income of a Canadian worker should increase at a faster rate than, or at least decrease at the same rate as that of his American counterpart in the years to come, so that we can maintain our competitive position?

subsubtopic: DISPOSABLE INCOME FOR CANADIAN EMPLOYEES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not want to make a statement that will cover the next ten years. I can only say that, at this moment, the Canadian economy has recovered its competitive position with the economy of the U.S. and that we will have to take all the necessary precautions so that we do not lose it.

Mr. Ir£nee Pelletier (Sherbrooke): Mr. Speaker, my question was for the Secretary of State, but in his absence I will direct it to the Deputy Prime Minister. Last Saturday, two Canadian universities, the University of British Columbia, the western champion, and Queen's University, the eastern champion, were playing for the championship of Canadian university football. I would like to know why the CBC's French network did not televise this event which does much more for Canadian unity than the two old American films which were shown on that network?

subsubtopic: REASON CANADIAN U.F.C. FINAL NOT TELECAST

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING CHILD ABUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Justice. In his absence, perhaps his parliamentary secretary or the Solicitor General would answer the question.
My question deals with the social problem of child abuse. Section 43 of the Criminal Code says:

Every schoolteacher, parent or person standing in the place of a parent is justified in using force by way of correction ... if the force does not exceed what is reasonable-
The Tree Foundation of Canada, which represents children who are abused and are being beaten, also asks whether this matter is under consideration by the Justice Department, so that when Bill C-51 returns to this House there will be sections in the Code regarding sanctions and with reference to child abuse; also other sections to protect children of this nation.

speakeroldname: Mr. Claude-Andre Lachance (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING CHILD ABUSE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the matter of child abuse is of great concern to the minister. In that respect, one of the major concerns is related to the fact that given the very nature of the offences, most often they are not reported to police authorities. In that respect I would recall to the hon. member that on November 9, 1978, the subject matter of Bill C-204 in the name of the hon. member for St. John's East, respecting a Canadian bill of rights for children, was referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. I think this would provide hon. members of this House with a very good opportunity to express their concerns and make suggestions to the minister with a view to amending the Criminal Code accordingly.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING CHILD ABUSE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I could get a statement at a later date, either from the parliamentary secretary or the Minister of Justice, on this subject-in light of the fact that 1979 will be the International Year of the Child. Would they take a hard look at the sections to the Code and the new amendments thereto, so children will be protected against abuse and beating, a problem which is becoming very prevalent and which is on the increase in Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING CHILD ABUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that question as well as all those regarding the rights of children-and I refer particularly to the matter related to the custody of the children and the difficulties encountered by custodians to keep their children
when one of the spouses leaves the province concerned____all
questions respecting the rights of children are currently under study, and again I repeat that the proceedings of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs will provide a very good opportunity to examine those questions in detail and to make recommendations to the House.

speechtext:

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member would take the trouble to read the documentation tabled in the House Thursday night , on budget night, he would find the exact figures.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF NEW POSTAL RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to make a brief statement on motions, and in particular to say a few words about the Post Office and Post Office rates. As hon. members will recall, on October 20 when I tabled the 1978 Post Office annual report, I also gave a statement to the press noting that, for the first time since the fiscal year 1971-72, the upward trend in the Post Office deficit had been reversed. I attributed our improved financial picture to the rate increase in the previous fiscal year, and to improved mail volumes.
The rate changes actually began with the two-stage increases of September, 1976, and March, 1977, and continued with the rate change of April, 1978. They are part of a staged process, not only to narrow the gap between revenues and costs but also to restore an appropriate balance between postal revenues and general taxation required to offset the costs of providing postal services to Canadians.
That balance had been changing over the years, with the taxpayer paying a higher percentage of postal costs and the postal user paying less. The portion of postal costs in excess of revenues, subsidized by government from general taxation, averaged 13.7 per cent during the 1960s and early 1970s, with no year exceeding 20 per cent. But rapidly rising costs outstripped the growth in revenues, and by 1975-76 the percentage of costs funded by government had risen to 49 per cent. Rate increases help to shift the balance back in the other direction. In fiscal year 1976-77 the percentage of costs funded by the government declined to 42.8 per cent. In the fiscal year ending March, 1978, subsidization through general taxation declined to 37.2 per cent. By asking the postal user to pay more for his share of the cost of mailing a letter, we help to reduce the cost to the taxpayer while increasing it for those who are actively using the service.
[ Translation]
There are, of course, certain things that the Post Office cannot do. I cannot ask some Canadians to pay more for mailing their letters for the only reason that they live in one of the largest areas of the country far from cities or main transport systems. I cannot decide to serve some Canadians and not others because it would not be profitable.
November 20, 1978



The Post Office is a complex blend of service and business. Because it is a service the Post Office must provide basic, national mail coverage to all Canadians, wherever they live, for the same reasonable price. Rightfully, therefore, there must be some element of government funding to help provide this national service. But the public purse and the public patience both have limits. Because the Post Office is this hybrid of service and business, its stockholders, the people of Canada, have the right to expect that it will live by the same economic rules that govern any large business. That is the only way that the Post Office will keep its costs and revenue figures under control, and its demands on the pocketbooks of the taxpayers to a reasonable minimum.
On the costs' side of the ledger, wages and transportation continue as the major costs of doing business. For more than a year the Post Office has been cutting back on those budget items that do not contribute directly to the operational side of the business. This means stringent control over the use of man-years, less spending on administration, and limitations and cutbacks on some programs, and we are keeping at it daily.

Mr. Speaker, the transport of mail is another very costly factor of postal operations. The Post Office can act in some sectors where they can control costs, through energy saving, the use and design of vehicles. It is more difficult to control other transport sectors, because the rates are set by airlines, railways and shipping companies. At this time when the cost of fuel is constantly increasing, transport companies can hardly control their expenditures and that is reflected in their rates. [English]
Postal revenues are determined by mail volumes and postal rates. Mail volumes continue to increase, but at a low rate. Volumes for the past fiscal year were 5.9 billion pieces of mail, an increase of only 2.8 per cent over the previous year.
That leaves postal rates. Sensible and business-like measures to control costs, and vigorous action in the marketplace to increase volumes are contributing to an improved financial position. By themselves, however, these measures are not enough to bring down the size of the Post Office deficit. To be fully effective they must be coupled with rate action that will bring in more revenue.
We feel that an increase in postal rates is warranted at this time, Mr. Speaker. It could be viewed as a continuation of the process commenced in September, 1976, to restore an appropriate balance between postal revenues and the general taxation revenue needed to offset the costs of doing business. However, equally important, a postal rate increase now also will help to improve the financial position of the Post Office at a time when the department is preparing for the complex change-over to Crown corporation status. Accordingly, we propose to implement price increases to most classes of domestic and international mail to take effect at the beginning of the next fiscal year, April 1, 1979.

Mr. Speaker, all hon. members are aware that the Canadian Post Office service, which used to be one of the most efficient in the world, in recent times has fallen upon less happy days. ETnfortunately the Post Office Department has become the butt of a lot of humour across the nation doday.
I do not think the statement which the Postmaster General (Mr. Lamontagne) made in the House today will do anything to enhance the reputation of Canada Post, at a time when it is most urgently needed. As I listened to his presentation, I realized that it was almost a detailed repetition of the statement made in the House one year ago almost to the day. On November 21, 1977, his predecessor, the present Solicitor General (Mr. Blais), made a statement. That was almost identical to the one we heard today. If this type of procedure continues, successive postmasters general should dust off the old speech and rise in their places to table it as read.
At the outset of my remarks this afternoon I want to make the point that something much more positive than this annual, ritualistic increase in postal rates must take place if Canada is to have the quality of postal service which is urgently needed. I admit that the statement last year was a little more realistic than the one made today by the Postmaster General, because it indicated that there were some real problems which had to be be dealt with if we were to bring the growing deficit into line.
The Postmaster General indicated that there were two sources of revenue: volumes of mail and increased subsidies from general revenue. Unfortunately over the past decade the balance has been going in the opposite direction, as between the positive and negative. The subsidies from taxpayers' revenue have been going up, and the volumes have been decreasing. This point was made in specific terms last year when the then postmaster general mentioned, because of the growing problems in the Post Office, that the projected volumes of first class mail, which is the real revenue earner, were down by one billion pieces. Also he made the specific point that the parcel post volume was back to the level it had been 20 years ago. By personal investigation I know that situation has not improved during the past year.
If anyone visits the huge Gateway plant in Toronto, he will find that the mechanized parcel sorting facility, which still has to be automated, is not functioning as intended. Instead of having increased volumes, which might have derived from improved marketing procedures, most of the parcel post, except for experimental runs which are being conducted in order to keep the computers in operation-

If he visits the plant, he will find out for himself that the computers are not functioning as originally intended. Because his constituency is in that area, the hon. member knows that the Post Office has rented the Canadian Arsenal facilities in order to process the parcels manually, rather than using the expensive ma-

chinery and computers which were supposed to handle the mail at this time.
The essence of the Postmaster General's statement this year introduces a new philosophy into Post Office financing. Referring to the announced increases he said the following:
They are part of a staged process, not only to narrow the gap between revenues and costs, but also to restore an appropriate balance between postal revenues and general taxation required to offset the costs of providing postal services to Canadians.
That is a new philosophy for financing the Canadian Post Office. It is almost a new mandate, as I am sure the hon. gentleman is aware that the mandate prescribed in Post Office regulations is to the effect that the Post Office is to provide postal service to the people of Canada at reasonable rates and at a standard of service adequate to meet their needs without incurring subsidies from general revenue.
The Postmaster General speaks optimistically of the declining deficit. I have the appropriate figures before me as compiled by the Canadian Tax Foundation in its report for 197778. This makes interesting reading.
In 1970 the Post Office Department registered a surplus of $14.3 million. The Post Office was then living within its mandate, providing an efficient service without incurring subsidies from general revenue. In 1971 there was a deficit of $31 million. In 1972 the deficit was $9.5 million. In 1973 the deficit increased to $26.4 million. In 1974 the deficit was $111.2 million. In 1975 the deficit was $252.4 million. In 1976 the deficit took a great leap to $468.9 million. In 1977 the deficit was $488.8 million, almost half a billion, and the estimated deficit for the current fiscal year, as indicated by the Postmaster General's own figures, has soared to over one half a billion, or $524 million. That is a pretty bad picture, as I am sure the hon. gentleman would agree, and these figures are from the Canadian Tax Foundation report. Coincidentally, they parallel the years this administration has been in power.
This is typical of the pattern of rising costs, soaring inflation, and other difficulties that have befallen the Canadian economy during the past ten years of the present Liberal administration.
In the few minutes that remain let me indicate to the Postmaster General that much more positive policies will have to be instituted if we are to reverse this unhappy state of affairs. This is not the first time the official opposition has outlined these matters in the House. The minister refers to a Crown corporation requiring additional infusions of money from the treasury. I suggest that does not necessarily have to be so.
As we have pointed out on several occasions, the Crown corporation method of organization and administration in the Post Office has been operating in the United Kingdom now for almost a decade. It was instituted in 1969 after very careful study and reports, both parliamentary and private. This is something we have been urging for the past several years in order that we can get at the facts.
November 20, 1978

Following this institution of the Crown corporation system in the United Kingdom in 1969, almost immediately there was a strike. That strike took place in 1971, so Crown corporations do not represent the solution to all the problems of the Post Office. This was a strike in that newly formed Crown corporation in the United Kingdom as a result of management failing to consult with unions on mechanization and automation programs. The process of mechanization was slowed down in the interests of labour-management relations.
Management and the unions came together, along with the postal users, in advisory committees where there was constant and continuous consultation. Training programs were instituted for supervisors and shop stewards in order that problems would be resolved on the plant floor as they arose rather than being allowed to accumulate in thousands of grievances as they have in Canada where there are some 10,000 plus grievances clogging up the present grievance process. Parliamentary investigations were organized on a regular basis to get at the root causes of problems in the British Post Office. The experiment of industrial democracy has been instituted, and this has induced in the British Post Office a spirit of co-operation rather than confrontation, and has resulted in returning the British Post Office to its former efficiency.
I maintain that exactly the same happy situation could obtain in Canada if the government would only provide the necessary leadership. The British Post Office is living within its mandate, showing a surplus of $83 million in postal operations at the present time.
My final suggestion to the Postmaster General is that he must do something about creating happier relationships with postal users. We have pursued this subject in a series of debates in the House in the last year, specifically regarding the method used by the government in increasing postal rates.
The Post Office Act, section 10, says this must be done by the authority of parliament through a formal legislative amendment. This was sustained by the Standing Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments. As a result of the arbitrary procedure on the part of the Post Office Department one of the major postal users in Canada, periodical publishers, took the government to the Supreme Court. They lost the first round but are now appealing. I am not going to discuss that in any more detail today other than to point out that this is no way to create good customer relationships, with customers having to take the government to court because of the arbitrary manner in which it has increased their costs.
I am sure we all understand why the Canada Post Office is in such difficult straits today, and why it is not working as an efficient operation. Just a month ago we had the last confrontation between labour and management in the Post Office. I had hoped the Postmaster General might have used the opportunity of this statement to report some positive developments. The moment of truth is now upon the Postmaster General and the government. We have reached a point of no return.
If the Postmaster General thinks that the establishment of a Crown corporation will be the sunnum bonum, or a universal solution to all his problems, he is sadly mistaken. We insist

that there must be a parliamentary inquiry so that the people who are most vitally concerned with postal services, the unions, the customers or postal users, will have a chance to appear before that committee to express their concerns. We are confident that if this sort of dialogue or consultation takes place, and if an atmosphere of co-operation replaces the present atmosphere of confrontation, we can restore the postal service to its position of high efficiency.

It seems to me there ought to be a moratorium on any rate increases until this Crown corporation is put in place and is able to take a look at the needs of the Post Office and the way in which improvements can be made in service to the taxpayers of Canada. The way this whole system is going to work should be examined.
1 know that the minister, in the twilight of his postmaster generalship, wants to feel important at this point. We can all appreciate that, and an ego massaging is going on right now. It is of some significance that this part of the budget debate was delayed to some degree by the introduction of a statement by the Postmaster General (Mr. Lamontagne), dealing with the situation in the Post Office.
