Now, after ten years of the government's continuance in office, it is running at a deficit of nearly half a billion dollars. Indeed, it proposes to pass the burden of that deficit along to ordinary Canadians who can least afford it. These ordinary Canadians have been counting upon the mail as a reasonable service.
This is not the first time this sort of thing has been done. It is precisely the same situation as in the case of who pays for the mistakes made by government in terms of its Taj Mahal and air transportation policies. The government built airports like Mirabel and others in the country, which were far beyond the needs of the nation. Then it passed the burden along, as the minister proposed in his budget the other night, to ordinary Canadians who are required to fly. As a spokesman for Quebecair indicated the other night, it ensures that the particular and hardest burden lies upon those Canadians living in some of the smaller centres of the country, who fly in and out of Newfoundland, Atlantic Canada and northern Ontario. They will be paying more regularly that kind of extra burden than will citizens who fly in and out of some of the larger metropolitan airports of the country.
The series of events in relation to the budget would have almost comic character to them, if they were not so serious. We have a Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) who is introducing in effect his third budget; at least his third new pair of shoes in 14 months.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Second.
The Budget-Mr. Clark

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is the minister talking about a pair of shoes or the budget?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The shoes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Both.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Both. I want the record straight.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Naturally I am reluctant to accept the minister's judgment on matters relating to the economy, but on matters relating to a pair of shoes I am prepared to trust his assessment.
I understand that the other night the Minister of Finance in speaking to television, or the enemy as the government characterizes them, said that he will not bring down another budget before an election. I imagine the emphasis was upon his not introducing another budget, because there is some very real suspicion on this side of the House that there will be another budget and another minister before we go to an election some time in the spring after five years of delay.
Another element of the comic character of what has been going on has been that the minister has three major stimulants to his credit. The first was the two-month tax holiday which was effective the beginning of this year. It was supposed to help increase our gross national product. Indeed, the GNP went up by .7 per cent in the first quarter. Then he talked about his employment tax credit, which was the second stimulant he was to introduce. It was to provide 50,000 new jobs for Canadians. Well, it is providing 8,000 new jobs for Canadians. The minister is wrong by approximately 85 per cent. Once again, the six-month wonder of the reduction in provincial sales tax was timed not to boost the economy but to attempt to boost the prospects of the Liberal party in the election. As the need for stimulus becomes more acute as winter comes on, that kind of stimulus is withdrawn.
As I will indicate later on in my remarks, we are left in a situation where for the remaining months of this year-the hard months, the winter months-there will be less stimulus provided by the government for economic growth in the country than there was in the relatively easy months prior to the termination of the provincial sales tax arrangement.
Again it is the minister whose forecasts are always wrong. In fact he is so wrong in his forecasts, I would suggest that after his defeat in the next federal election he might want to move to Toronto where he can support the Argonauts. I know of no other group of people who are so often wrong in their forecasts.
Some lion. Members: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Again in terms of being frank with the House of Commons, this is a minister who has brought in statements we find difficult to accept as complete. We know, for example, that when he talks about his deficit figures, those deficit figures exclude at least $854 million in liabilities incurred by

November 20, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Clark
the Government of Canada through three Crown corporations alone. We do not know, because he will not tell the whole truth to the people of Canada, the full extent of the rest of the obligations that have been incurred by this government or its agencies but which count against the accounts and the credit of Canada and which should be considered as part of the deficit this government has built up.
Finally, sir, in terms of the comedy we face, we have the explanations, which vary, as to just who exactly is at fault here. One moment it is the weather that has caused all these problems in the Canadian economy, then it is the Arabs, then from time to time it is Rene Levesque, and from time to time it is me. The Minister of Finance said I was causing all the problems in the country. Now he has discovered another enemy. It is the media that is causing all the problems in the country. Indeed, if you read his budget, or if you were listening to him the other night, you will have noticed he has one more cause for Canada's economic problems. Who are these people who are working against the interests of Canada? They are the coal miners of the United States of America. They are the culprits, the coal miners of the United States who are causing all the problems we are having here.
I suppose the minister read that in his conflicts with John L. Lewis, Harry Truman, who was a legitimate street fighter, came out on top. Even though the spirit of Harry Truman does not really linger on over there, and John L. Lewis is gone, perhaps the minister thought some luck might rub off if he too were to ascribe all Canada's economic difficulties to the members of the United Mine Workers of another country.
In fact, the reality in this country is that other nations with whom we should be compared are doing considerably better than we are, and the reality is that we have the highest unemployment rate in the western industrial world-a country with the potential of Canada-that our inflation rate is second only to Italy among nations in the industrial world, and that those problems were caused not by some foreigners, not by some coal miners in some other country, but were caused by the incompetence of this government on the other side of this House.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What is perhaps most alarming to Canadians is that we recognize now that, particularly with the decline in the United States and with the absence of any stimulus, no one outside this country is going to help this country up. The only people who can build this country up are Canadians themselves, and the only way they can do that is with leadership from the government. This government indicated the other night that it intends no leadership at all. So the obligation is clearly upon us, and it is an obligation we will accept as soon as the Prime Minister finds the courage to move from making speeches to calling elections.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Canadians have that choice.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I understand the interjection from an hon. member from, of all places, Scarborough, was that Canadians
[Mr. Clark.)
had the obligation to make that choice. Well, the Canadians in Scarborough made that choice not long ago.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There are some aspects of this budget that we think valuable. We are pleased to see that, after rejecting it for a long time, the government has finally accepted our view that there should be some movement toward a reduction of the manufacturing sales tax at the federal level, although we think it should have been more selective in its cuts rather than across the board. We are very pleased that the government has finally moved to encourage activity again in the creation of jobs in the mining industry in the country. I was a little amused to note the minister said in his budget address, "I want to take the lead here." We know what happened. The minister was with the provincial ministers of finance who made it very clear to him that unless the federal government stopped putting obstacles in the path of mining development, there would be no help from the provinces. It was the pressure from the provinces that caused this government finally to make the changes that will perhaps create some growth in the mining industry in Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Again we are pleased to see that the government has begun to move toward the encouragement of research and development. This government, which under the former Prime Minister, Mr. Pearson, as one of its first acts began the discontinuance of the incentives to research and development that had been introduced by the hon. Georges Hees when he was the minister of trade and commerce in the Diefenbaker government, is moving again in this direction. The Conservative government brought in the incentives which the Liberal government then abandoned for ten long years. We are pleased to see them coming back.
I have to say to the minister that I am sorry the government has not accepted the detail of my advice in this regard, and that the government is not giving more attention to directing the research and development incentives in this country toward a focusing upon those companies or innovators who will deal with specific Canadian problems or specific Canadian potential, because our R and D problem in this country is aggravated by the fact that there is so much leakage to head offices elsewhere. What we need in terms of an effective research and development policy and approach in this country is a policy which will focus in upon those Canadian innovators who will face Canadian problems and deal with Canadian potential and not be tempted to leak this away to head offices in some other countries.
I have indicated that over-all there are some specific matters we find of value, not the least because we proposed many of them. We are getting used to that on this side of the House. In over-all terms this is a budget that provides no real stimulus. My colleague, the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies), got the minister to admit today that its purpose is not to deal with inflation, and its purpose is not to create jobs for Canadi-
November 20, 1978

ans, because it is not going to deal effectively with inflation and it is going to create new unemployment in Canada rather than create jobs for Canadians. The government's purpose is simply to try to survive.
I see the minister holding up three fingers and I will come to what he means by those three fingers a little bit later. The fact is that those three fingers should really be taken as indicating strike one, strike two, and strike three.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What we have here is a government with a budget that has no real stimulus, a budget with a larger deficit, the effect of which will be stagnation, as usual, of the Canadian economy. It is a budget that promises, as I say, to create more unemployment. We already have the worst record in unemployment in the industrialized world, but his minister is going to make it worse.

The Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) mentioned the creation of some 250,000 new jobs for next year. If the rate of real growth is between 4 per cent and 4'A per cent, this prediction-and we must admit that the Minister of Finance has not been very successful up to now with his predictions- this prediction, should it come true, will only make certain that a still larger number of people will be unemployed because it has already been established that 325,000 new people will join the labour force. This figure has already been confirmed, and the new incentives contained in the budget will create at most
250,000	new jobs. Who will look after the 75,000 other people without jobs?
The right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stated recently in Toronto that with his Quebec members he can represent Quebeckers best. The problem stems from the fact that the right hon. Prime Minister is taking Quebeckers for granted, and based on this assumption, he comes up with all sorts of measures which create unemployment. How could he speak on behalf of workers when unemployment is particularly severe in the province of Quebec? What is needed are new members who will increase possibilities for Quebec, namely Quebec Progressive Conservative party members who will not accept policies or budgets conducive to unemployment. All I can say, Mr. Speaker, is that if there are unemployed in Quebec, the Liberal members will be among them.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That's a good punch line.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am very pleased that my friend from Quebec got the first punch line, because when the election comes he will be sure to get the second punch line.
The Budget-Mr. Clark

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The excuse that we are being given here for a budget that stimulates nothing at all is that the government has very limited room to manoeuvre. Well, Mr. Speaker, who limited the room to manoeuvre of the Government of Canada? Indeed, how good were the choices which were made in that limited room to manoeuvre? We are in a deep deficit position today in this country, and the question has to be asked: why we are in that deep deficit position? Did it just happen overnight? Did somebody else do it? Was it really the coal miners, the Arabs, or somebody else? Or was it, perhaps, successive ministers of finance, some of them now reduced to writing memoranda, who have occupied the treasury benches of the government opposite?
Let us take a look at what happened in years when the people of Canada did not need spending by government for economic stimulus. In some of those years this Liberal government deepened the deficit of Canada by increasing budgetary spending 17.3 per cent in 1974, 18.8 per cent in 1975, 26.5 per cent in 1976, and 19.3 per cent in 1977. You speak about limited room to manoeuvre. Now you know who limited the room. It was yourself and the other ministers in the Trudeau Liberal government of Canada who have been mismanaging the economy of Canada for the last ten years.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: One problem that we face as a country is that this government has developed a virtually incurable spending habit. But it has also dangerously crippled some of the natural strengths of the country. We talked earlier about research and development. I see the new member for Westmount (Mr. Johnston) is in his seat. I want to say one thing about his predecessor, a man I generally admired. In my judgment, one of the most dangerous decisions for Canada ever to be taken by this government was the decision that went out over the name of the previous member for Westmount, when he was minister responsible, that we in this country will buy our technology elsewhere, because by abandoning the responsibility for research and development and innovation in Canada, we drove hundreds, indeed thousands of innovators, researchers and scientists out of this country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Unfortunately, sir, that policy is being carried on today as the Government of Canada shuts down research station after research station across the country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not so with telecommunications.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Telecommunications is an interesting case because of what has happened in the field of telecommunications.
Let me come to another Field where the Canadian capacity to grow has been crippled by this government, that of small business. We now have a government department that deals

November 20, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Clark
with government bureaucracy. Government service to small business in this country is to try to cut down some of the government paper with which the government has been smothering small business for years. That has been the total effect of their policies up until this budget. There are a few more proposals that they are following now.
Clearly, what is needed here is a far more comprehensive small business encouragement policy. What is needed here is what I have proposed several times across this country, namely, a tax incentive in the form of a tax credit up to a maximum of $5,000 a year available to those Canadians who are prepared to put their money into Canadian-owned small business. We need that, we need it now, and it should have been in this budget. It will be in ours.
We need to move quickly to give permission to small businessmen to form consortia for competition internationally. I know that is part of a stillborn bill that this government introduced, as it introduces so many stillborn bills. But that provision should be taken out of the bill and put into law right now so that we can allow and encourage small business in Canada to get out into the world and build upon their industry and their opportunity, and so they can form the kind of consortia in Canada with which they have to compete abroad.
Again, sir, this government has to begin to take seriously its obligations, followed in other countries like Japan and the United States-countries with which we have to compete-to shape its purchasing policy in a way that does not buy everything from the government's friends in the big corporations but instead extends a certain strong proportion of its purchases to small Canadian entrepreneurs and small businesses. Again that is what we are going to do as a government, given that opportunity.
There have been a number of other fields, sir, in which the actions of this government have crippled the Canadian capacity to compete in the world. We have spoken of the mining industry in which we have lost thousands of jobs as a result of stagnation stemming from the conflict between governments in regard to mining policy. Another field that has clearly been damaged severely in this country is agriculture, which used to be among the priorities when Canadians went abroad to negotiate but is now a matter whose interests are traded away.
I could give many, many other examples, Mr. Speaker. Think of the negative impact upon this country of the tremendous investment outflow. In the 30 years prior to 1974 money used to come into this country. This was a country to which people came from around the wide world to invest. But in the last three years more Canadian money has been invested outside Canada than foreign money has been invested in Canada. That is a mark of the lack of confidence that investors here and around the world have in this government.
That is some of the damage that has been done, Mr. Speaker. The Trudeau government has made Canada's position very difficult. Given that difficult position, it is now making the wrong choices in regard to what we need to do to improve our situation. The government claims now to acknowledge the need to combine a policy of restraint and one of

stimulus. It claims to acknowledge that, although I remember the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) saying earlier this year, on February 22, 1978, when being pressed from this side of the House to make reductions, "We are cutting the fat wherever we can". That is what he said then, and the implication was that there was nothing more that they could cut. That was before the first of the series of nocturnal admissions on August 1, when the Prime Minister announced that he had discovered these new areas in which economies could be made.
The fact, sir, is that throughout this budget, indeed throughout the term of office of this government, there has been too little restraint and too little stimulus. I want to speak about restraint. The restraint announced on August 1 reminds me of the one consistent element of the government's economic policy, and that is that when the government has anything important to announce it sends the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) out of the country. On August 1 the government sent him to Japan. When the Minister of Finance finally decided on a budget date, they sent the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce down to the Caribbean. I understand there have been other ministers on that side who have been travelling around the Caribbean lately; the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Allmand) did. I am given to understand that some of his officials in his department thought that he should have taken along the expert who knew what was being discussed at the conference that he attended, and that they took up a collection to send the relevant expert,

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That was the commissioner for patents.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, the commissioner for patents. And knowing the esteem in which the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce is held by public servants, I would not be surprised if his public servants took up a collection to try to keep him in the Caribbean.
The government announced a program of restraint by surprise on August 1. A lot of us were wondering what pattern was going to be followed in this period of restraint. We wondered what would be the priorities, what would be the guidelines that would lead the government to decide where to cut and where not to cut. It was very, very difficult to come to any sensible conclusion, looking at where the cuts were made. I thought 1 had discovered a pattern at one point. I thought that they were cutting where the ministers were weakest and that it was simply a matter of who around the table could argue most strongly for their private empire.
I know it is difficult, Mr. Speaker, to try to make any comparison of strength and weakness in a cabinet like this one, but I thought for a while that that was the standard. I think I was wrong. I think it is increasingly becoming clear now that the Government of Canada-and this is a very serious matter-applied restraint to projects that it knew were popular enough or necessary enough that there was going to be very strong protest. Ministers wanted to go out into the country and say, "Look, we are restraining; we are cutting back. How can you tell we are cutting back? Sure, we are taking airlines to
November 20, 1978

Grey Cup games and things like that, but how can you tell we are cutting back? Listen to the screaming. Look at the people who are complaining". In other words, what they were interested in when they established their list of targets for restraint was not the size of the saving; they were concerned about the size of the protest. If the protests were strong the government could take that as proof of its own seriousness about restraint.
That, like so much that was followed by this government, was a very short term strategy. The proof that it is a short term strategy is that the government has already been forced to back down on some of the particularly foolish proposals for restraint, proposals such as the phasing out of forestry stations, the phasing out of weather ships on the west coast, the phasing out of weather forecasting which could have meant a matter of life and death in the province of my colleague from St. John's.
The real proof that the so-called restraint of this government was a fraud, the real proof of the fraudulent nature of that restraint, was given to the House in the eight days immediately before the minister brought down his budget. It became clear then that this remains a government that, given the opportunity to extend its own control over aspects of the Canadian community where it should have control, is prepared to spend without restraint. It did that in the case of Nordair and the attempt at the Pacific Petroleums Ltd. acquisition.
What is significant and what indicates how fraudulent this commitment to restraint is, are the things the government has not cut. First of all, there has been a very insignificant cut, certainly not as significant as is possible, in the practice of contracting out. This is a very dangerous practice, dangerous to our system of government because it allows a government that wants to, to get around the protection against patronage, to get around the protection against incompetence that is built into the Public Service Commission, that is built into the system of ensuring we have a government that makes its decisions in accord with the facts and not in accord with improper pressures, and makes its appointments with regard to competence and not with regard to friendship.
There has been an immense increase in contracting out by this government, Mr. Speaker. Indeed the cost of contracting out has increased six and one half times in the period this government has been in office, from $214.9 million in 1968 to $1,424 billion in the latest year. That is a six and one-half fold increase in contracting out.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hear some protests from ministers on the other side. There is no question that there may well be some areas in which contracting out makes sense, but there is also no question at all-it is always easy to tell when one strikes close to the bone, Mr. Speaker, because ministers start to complain. It is also very, very clear that there has been an immense capacity for abuse not only of spending but of controls to ensure that there is protection against patronage. That capacity was there, and I suggest that if this was a
The Budget-Mr. Clark
government that was very seriously concerned about practicis-ing restraint we would have had some significant cuts in the practice of contracting out.
One of the areas where there has not been a dramatic indication of a determination to have restraint has been in relation to that invention of the Prime Minister in the Canadian political system-in effect, I believe, a cancer in the Canadian system-the building up of the strength of the Privy Council office and the Prime Minister's office at the expense of the cabinet, at the expense of parliament, at the expense of democracy in this country. During the first six months of fiscal 1979, the year of restraint, spending on the Privy Council office has increased by 86 per cent. The Privy Council office hired 80 new people last year. The Prime Minister's office hired 54. Perhaps these people are all necessary; perhaps they are the people who will administer restraint in the country. I cannot be sure about that, but what is clear is that the one agency of government that has been most free of restraint has been the agency that encircles the Prime Minister. In terms of establishing policy direction in this country it has taken the place that used to be occupied by cabinets when cabinets were filled with strong people determined to represent the interests of the regions from which they came.
As I mentioned, Mr. Speaker, the most dramatic example of the fraudulent nature of restraint came in the two most recent acquisitions. I say most recent because we do not know what they are going to try to buy up next. They went into the private market to spend $28 million on an airline. They say they are going to get rid of it after a year, but they have said that before about other Crown agencies. They said that four or five years ago-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about Pacific Western?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I see the Minister of Finance is suggesting that the Government of Canada is now taking the government of Alberta as a model. I would simply suggest to him that, if he is going to do that, there are a number of better areas than in relation to the acquisition of aircraft. I say to him also, Mr. Speaker-

-and it might be essential for me to point out the fact that one of the differences between the situation with the airline owned by the government of Alberta and the airline bought by the Government of Canada lies in the fact that other people were able to buy Nordair-

And that was not the case in the Pacific Western Airline's situation. Nonetheless, the government practised restraint by spending $28 million on an airline it does not need, an airline for which a private purchaser was available. It was not exactly a fire sale in the case of Nordair because Great Lakes Airlines Limited or other purchasers would have bought it. The Government of Canada, however, with the interest in control that was so clear in the speech made the other day by the Minister of Transport and Justice (Mr. Lang) and of the Wheat Board

November 20, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Clark
and anything else he can get his hands on-that instinct for control led this government to buy an airline it did not need, in absolute disregard for the restraint aspects of its policy.
Having struck out in their attempt to acquire Husky Oil for Petro-Can, they looked around and found another oil company. They incurred obligations of $ 1.4 billion in this period of restraint which they have tried to hide. One of the things that interests me about Petro-Can-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Tell it the way it is.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am telling it the way it is. I am pleased that once again the good doctor, who served as such an effective foil for my colleague, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) the other night, has taken an interest in this debate. If he knows the oil industry-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Do not get personal or I will.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Tell us about unemployment in the Niagara peninsula.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The truth about Petro-Can, Mr. Speaker, is that since it became clear a government would be elected that intends to have the state move out of activities in which the state should not belong, the main exploration activity of Petro-Can has been in the boardrooms of other companies. Their means of discovering oil is to buy a company that has some, and buy it at the potential cost to Canada, the incurring of obligations by Canada of $1.4 billion.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is very difficult for me with the hon. member for Welland (Mr. Railton) shouting from across the way. I know that he does stand up to speak in this House from time to time, and I hope he will be able to influence his colleagues in the Liberal party to give him a place to stand and speak so that he will not have to make his whole speech by interrupting mine.
The other night the hon. member for York-Simcoe indicated that the great significance of buying an airline that was not necessary and an oil company that was not necessary is that the purchases indicate how wrong are the priorities of this government. In our judgment, we should be divesting ourselves of some of these Crown agencies we do not need and putting that money back into use in ways that will stimulate the Canadian economy. Even if the government does not accept that view, even if it does not want to rely on the private sector to generate growth and jobs in the country as we do, even if it wants to stay true to its own statist philosophy, surely it could have found better use for $1.5 billion than buying an oil company and an airline it does not need. Surely there are old age pensioners in this country who could have made better use of that money than the American owners of Pacific Petroleums.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Hear, hear!
[Mr. Clark.)

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Surely there are a number of Canadians looking for homes who could put that money to better use. But instead this government, so intent on controlling everything it can, ignores the elderly Canadians and those Canadians who need homes, ignores the taxpayer in this country, ignores the legitimate priorities in Canada-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No taxpayers' money.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Let us try to get some quiet in here because the Minister of Finance has made an important point. He has shouted from his seat that there is no Canadian taxpayers' money involved here. There is an obligation on the part of the Government of Canada to the extent of $1.4 billion. That obligation, if it comes to be honoured, will have to be paid by taxpayers' money. I am asked about the assets. I think it is understood that there has been a remarkable difference between the quoted market value for Pacific Petroleums shares and the value that is being paid by the Government of Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about AGTL and Husky? The margin was bigger.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The minister is making another speech from his seat. I heard him, but it is difficult to hear because there is so much shouting from over there. I heard him talk about Husky. I want to say something about Husky because the Prime Minister of Canada-outside this House naturally-defended the acquisition of Pacific Petroleums by saying that it was in the interests of Canadian ownership. The Husky deal showed that there is more than one way to acquire Canadian ownership of international oil companies. The private sector will do it when the private sector has an opportunity to do it. And speaking for this party, we would prefer to see private ownership in the energy industry accomplished by private Canadian entrepreneurs going out and building for themselves.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We believe there has to be a combination of real restraint and real stimulus. I want to spell out again the elements of the restraint program that we will introduce as a government. First of all, it will be permanent restraint, not the kind of cosmetic restraint that this government has talked about. It will be permanent restraint accomplished in the following ways, and accomplished in accord with three principles.
First, we will permanently reduce the operating costs of government. We will do that by not hiring new public servants when vacancies become open due to death, retirement, or by moving away. We have an immense respect for the capacity and ability of serving Canadian public servants. We know that many of them are frustrated and underutilized. We intend to give to Canadian public servants the opportunity to move into positions of responsibility in the Canadian public service, to which access is now denied them.
November 20, 1978

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We will follow that policy of attrition in public service size and of calling upon the best from Canadian public servants. That will result in a net reduction in the size and the cost of the Government of Canada. Second, we will introduce into the practice of the government and Parliament of Canada, some of the cost control techniques which this nation has been without for far too long. We are going to introduce zero based budgeting throughout the Government of Canada. We are going to return to the House of Commons, this parliament which was established to represent and protect the interests of all Canadians, all the power to control government spending.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I was not a member of this House at the time, but I am familiar with one of the first items on the agenda of this government, when it was first elected in 1968. Indeed, it forced a measure through parliament in 1969. I use the word "forced" advisedly because for the first time in the history of British parliamentary tradition anywhere in the world, this government changed the rules of parliament by the use of closure.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They did that, sir, with one goal in mind. The goal was to take away from the House of Commons the power to control government spending.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not true.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Absolutely true, and the record makes it clear. Recognizing that while it took the Trudeau government less than a year to undo the principles which were established centuries ago, we intend in forming a new government to give the highest priority, to bringing back reforms that will allow the then Leader of the Opposition-I do not know if the member for Mount Royal will hold to that office or open it up to the queue that is already forming behind him-to choose two departments whose estimates will be examined without any restriction of time. The choice will be made after all estimates have been prepared, so that estimates will be prepared in the expectation of the kind of scrutiny which is the only guarantee of responsible government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Again, the third principle we will follow in terms of ensuring there is real restraint will be to get the government out of areas where it does not belong. Earlier today I talked about Petro-Canada. Petro-Canada is one of the classic cases of what can go wrong when the government gets in where it should not be. It is justified as being a window on the oil industry. I would not be surprised if other companies competing with Petro-Canada, particularly as Petro-Can now moves to larger and larger status, are less prepared and more reluctant to make confidential information available to a government regulator which they know is a regulator on one day and
The Budget-Mr. Clark
the owner of a competitive company the next day. I would not be surprised if it is having a negative effect and closing the window which the National Energy Board already has. That is one point in relation to Petro-Can.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The French, the English, The Netherlands, everyone. You are of the sixteenth century.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Minister of Finance tells us there is a justification for the government's policy, that is, that other countries have oil companies.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Other countries have monsoons, other countries have state police agencies, other countries have censorship rules, other countries have a number of things. Because they exist in other countries is no reason for them to exist here.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The standard which should be established and guide government decisions here is not what is good for other countries but what is good for this particular country, Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There are two other reasons. I will not debate the whole Petro-Can matter. This determination to become involved in the private economy is dangerous. One of the reasons has to do with the conflict of interest between a government which owns one company and sets the rules for all companies. That is most evident in relation to the northern land regulations where the northern land regulations have been changed, quite clearly to give specific advantage to the company the government owns. It is just like anybody in this room who has a son who plays softball or baseball, if anyone has a daughter who plays hockey-as they should be in Barrie,-you know very well that if you were called upon to umpire a game there would be a strong suspicion among other parents and players that you are giving preference to your son or daughter. That is exactly the situation here. There is evidence of this because the northern land regulations have been changed explicitly to confer special advantage on the company the government owns.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The other day in this House we had another indication of a conflict of interest. It was a conflict of interest of a very invidious kind because it put a leading and outstanding public servant in a very difficult position. I speak, of course, of the deputy minister of finance who is required by law to participate in confidential government budget decisions and is also required by law to sit as a member of the board of directors of Petro-Canada. He was put in the invidious position of knowing what Petro-Canada was going to do at a time when he might have been seized of knowledge about the budget. No Canadian public servant should be put in that situation. The minister is nervous. I ask him to check-

November 20, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Clark

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, I would like to reply. It is dicey. Make an accusation if you can.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: One sign of panic and decay on the other side is that every time an issue arises, they say, "Make a charge". Well, I will make the charge that I have made. The Government of Canada has put the Deputy Minister of Finance in a very invidious postion. That is the charge. The people against whom the charge lies are the Government of Canada. The reason it is subject to that charge is because it is so determined to control so many of the activities in this country that would function better if they operated without the heavy hand of government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Naturally our view of achieving restraint by getting the government out of activities where it should not be is opposed by some other parties in this chamber. It is opposed for different reasons.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He is running away.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If the Minister of Finance cannot make it as a shoe salesman, he will certainly make it as a humourist.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There are two different kinds of objections. The Government of Canada, the Liberal party, which speaks most eloquently from its seat and to its discredit and sorrow speaks most eloquently by its actions, because by its actions it is known, as the last series of by-elections in this country demonstrated so dramatically, is concerned about divesting control of any of the more than 300 Crown corporations.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Three hundred and eighty-five.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There are 385 Crown corporations which they like to control. It was very interesting listening to the Minister of Transport the other day talking about the process of de-regulation in the air industry in the United States which has brought down fares and increased usage, saying it would not work here. He said there are public interest factors which you have to consider. That is short for saying he does not want to let go of any of his control. That is really the philosophy of this government.
This is a highly statist government, and it is not for philosophic reasons. There are philosophic reasons to my left. It is because this government enjoys running things, even if it runs them badly.
The New Democratic Party are interested in public ownership because that is their ideology. It has been their ideology since the Regina manifesto. They have changed very few of their views since the Regina manifesto. That is, nonetheless, a relatively legitimate reason. Certainly philosophy is a more legitimate reason for a statist approach to government than

simply a desire to keep your hands on everything that moves, which is the control orientation of the Liberal party.
In relation to the NDP, I have had a chance to look at the amendment they have introduced.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Subamendment.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As well as reading the Regina manifesto, it is beyond dispute that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has also read the rules of parliament. The effect of that subamendment is to strike out the objection which we in this party take to the incessant acquisition by the Government of Canada of ventures which are better operated by others. That is the deleting effect.
The adding effect is redundant. It talks about creating employment in the country. It is redundant to our motion because our motion makes it clear that what we believe is necessary is a stimulant budget. There is no question that that kind of stimulant which I and my colleagues have outlined for some time, many elements of which have been adopted by the government, would provide the employment that is called for explicitly in the NDP motion.
I might say a word about Crown corporations. There is no question that in a nation like this, young, large, still developing, still a place that has to attract capital and develop its own capacity to increase its investment capacity to do the things we want to do but cannot quite do, there is going to be a continuing need to have the state intervene from time to time. However, the rule must be that the government should intervene as a last resort because it needs to, not as a first resort because it wants to intervene. Indeed, that distinction led predecessors of mine in the leadership of this party to establish some of the great Crown corporations and Crown agencies in this country, corporations like the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and agencies like the Canadian Wheat Board. That is a tradition which is essential to this country.
There is no question at all that we must continue to have the state ready to move in as a last resort when the private sector cannot function. However, these Crown corporations and agencies established for one purpose at one point in time should not be above examination. We should look at them to see if they are doing what they were set up to do.
We should see if the country has matured to the stage where such activity is no longer as necessary as it once was. That is the approach that we in this party intend to take to a number of the activities in which the Government of Canada is now involved. We will do it directly in some cases, such as in relation to a Crown corporation like Petro-Can where our view is clear. We will do it by empowering this parliament through the sunset laws to examine the continuing need to exist of various Crown corporations and agencies so that we can improve those we keep and get rid of those that should not continue to be supported by public funds.
I can name some examples where it would be well to have a committee empowered with a sunset law, reviewing the need to keep as an acquisition something possessed by the Government
November 20, 1978

of Canada such as Canadian Arsenals, the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation and the Defence Construction Corporation. Do we need to keep those? Should we not be asking this kind of question rather than making the knee jerk reaction of, "Now that we have them, should not we hold them?"
Parliament should be acting now to reform activities like the Canadian Dairy Commission which has some areas that clearly need reform, as well as the pilotage authorities. Atomic Energy of Canada Limited clearly needs scrutiny and reform by this parliament. CIDA would benefit substantially from scrutiny and reform by this parliament, particularly in light of some of the recommendations of the Science Council, as would the Foreign Investment Review Agency.
Why should these be sacrosanct? Why should parliament be prevented from reviewing their usefulness and continued need to exist? Why should we put that prohibition upon ourselves at a time when it is so necessary for us to practice restraint and save the money of the taxpayers of Canada?

When I said that having partners was essential I was speaking of steps to restrain government expenditures; but today we also need strong incentives for barely half of the real economic possibilities in Canada are being developed. Our rate of unemployment is the highest of all industrialized countries; our rate of inflation exceeds all others with the exception of Italy. Almost all Canadian private forecasters claim that things will be no better next year.
In Canada, we can do much better than that. According to the Conference Board, even a rate of real growth of 4.75 per cent and a rate of unemployment of 5.5 per cent would increase the wealth of the nation by $41 billion within two years, wealth which could be used to generate new investments and new jobs. The Conference Board also believes that if those growth and job objectives were achieved this year and next year, federal and provincial government revenues would grow by over $13 billion, which would contribute immeasurably to restoring balance in the government accounts.
What we need above all is incentives. In the aggregate, our stimulants would include a decrease in federal income taxes of at least $2 billion in favour of Canadians who would spend that money quickly here in Canada; cuts in the mortgage rate and income tax up to fixed limits spread over a four-year period; a tax credit on investments for those Canadians who are willing to invest their money in small Canadian businesses; and specific steps to encourage research and development, to protect capital gains, to protect inventories against inflation and, in particular, to encourage regional development.
As I said earlier, the effect of the budget introduced by the minister the other night will actually be to reduce the stimulus for the remainder of the current fiscal year. The minister needed a tax cut of $750 million for the second half of fiscal
The Budget-Mr. Clark
1978-79 to maintain the stimulus which was given to the economy by provincial sales tax cuts. Instead of the $750 million which was needed, this budget provides only $300 million. That is by the minister's own admission. The stimulus is down for the remainder of this fiscal year. It is down, after the minister has failed to meet his April growth target. It is down at a time when we are heading into a winter of one million unemployed. At a time like that, the Trudeau government reduces the stimulus in the Canadian economy.
I want to talk for a moment about the budget process. I will not speak for much longer, but I want to talk about the budget process because part of what has gone wrong here in the last ten years is that this government has been so certain that it knew all the answers that it has moved away from people who might have other ideas and might have contributions and suggestions to make.
The minister has boasted that he had more consultation this time. He had a series of private and secret meetings across the country, and I congratulate him for that. That is a step forward, but it is still a step in the shadows. What should be happening is that this kind of consultation should be taking place here in the open. I say "here" advisedly because, before a budget is brought down, the obvious place for discussion of the economic climate and economic potential of this country is in a committee of the House of Commons. That is what we are here for. That is what parliament was established to do. If we were able to do that, we would be able to invite, to a committee of this House, the consumers' association, the manufacturers' association, the Canadian Labour Congress and all groups which have legitimate interests in national economic policy. We would be able to sit down with them, as well as with representatives of the C. D. Howe Institute, the Fraser Institute and a number of other private agencies which are concerned about economic policy. We would have public discussions which would increase and improve public understanding of the economic problems and the economic potential of this country.
Other countries do that, and we need to do that. As a government, we are going to do it as part of our reform of parliament.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
A reform which we will introduce will be the annual publication of five-year spending forecasts and five-year revenue forecasts of the Government of Canada. What is almost unbelievable and almost impossible for me to accept is that in the United States, in the United Kingdom and in Canada there are five-year revenue projections and five-year spending projections, that in the United States they are published, that in the United Kingdom they are published, but that in Canada under the Trudeau government they are kept secret.
Why are they kept secret? Why should parliament not know what public servants know when they set budget policy? Why should the people of Canada not know about the implications, five years down the line, of budget policy which is being

November 20, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Clark
brought in now? Why should there be so much secrecy? Why should Canadians be kept in the dark about the basis of national economic policy? There is no reason. This government, which has grown so old in office, is so captive to the old habit of secrecy that it simply will not break it.
I give to the people of Canada and to this House the commitment that after the next election we as a new government will break that bad habit and let the sun shine in on the five-year forecasts and projections on which national economic policy is based.
I think all of us in this parliament are concerned about how much, if anything, must be kept secret and how much can be made public. We must take a hard look at taking away part of the veil which now covers our budget-making process. We know that the way the United States deals with the problem of holding a potential special advantage because of special information is by making sure that all information is available to everybody. Here we keep all information from everybody. 1 think we must take a hard look at whether the system in the United States does not have more to recommend it than the system which has led us to so much economic difficulty here.
With regard to those technical changes in budgetary policy which can confer no positive or negative advantage or disadvantage, we in this party think that those matters should be discussed in public and that they should be moved out, from the preparation of this budget onward, into the open so that there can be that kind of consideration.
Unfortunately, this secrecy which has cast a shadow and a cloak over budgetary policy is pervasive in this government. In the budget documents there is a brief, seemingly innocuous but dangerous reference to some $300 million which the government of Canada is going to make available to those companies which are adversely affected by the negotiations at the Geneva round of GATT. The government knows what went on at GATT; parliament does not, the companies affected do not. The government does know, and the government is of the view that at least $300 million worth of damage was done to the Canadian public interest and to the interests of Canadian companies by what was negotiated away at GATT.
Part of the reason that that causes so much concern is that the industries whose lives and future are being affected by these negotiations at GATT have consistently been kept outside. Once again, other nations with economies far more complex than ours have found ways to ensure that industries whose lives are affected by tariff negotiations have a means of participating in those negotiations. That is not the case here.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They have had a lot of input.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The parliamentary secretary correctly says that they have had a lot of input, but they have had input up to a point, and then public servants-admittedly good people- have had theirs. The industries involved have been sent away, but there is no role in Canadian delegations, as there is in the delegations of other countries, for representatives of some of those industry groups to participate directly in the negotiations. One consequence is that not only do people live with the

certainty that the Government of Canada has concluded that there has been at least $300 million worth of damage done to the Canadian economy by the GATT negotiations, but also there is the suspicion that if somebody who knew more about an industry which was bargained away had been present at the table, then the injury done to that Canadian industry would not have occurred. That is the tragedy, and we must change our procedures to prevent that.
The basic weakness of this budget and, indeed, the basic weakness of this government is that it is standing pat. It is dealing with the past. It has no sense of the future of this country. In ten years the government has wasted and crippled some of the great building assets of Canada.
This budget promises us a deeper deficit and stagnation as usual. There is no excitement in this budget, and there is no excitement in this tired old government. There is no excitement about the potenital of this country, and this budget certainly offers no encouragement.
It is quite interesting to look at the threads which run through the language of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance. They talk about the problems Canada faces and about this being a difficult world. They talk about all the obstacles we face and about all the bad things which are in the atmosphere. The fact is if they would get out of their cocoons and visited this country, if they would stop apologizing about what they had done and began to look at what we can do as a people, they would realize that this is not a country beset by problems, but a country beset by opportunities and possibilities.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Nobody pretends that this is an easy country to govern, it never has been, but there is no question at all that Canada can be governed, that it can grow as an economy. What is necessary is to have a Government of Canada that is prepared to trust the people of Canada more than this government does. There has to be a determination to encourage the instinct to build which is part of Canadian life, whether it is evident in a company like Great Lakes Air-which wanted to buy the airline which the government bought-in a company like Alberta Gas Trunk Line-which moved in and ensured Canadian ownership in a far preferable way to having Petro-Can move in-or, indeed, whether it is evident in the aspirations of countless Canadians across the country who simply want to own, buy or build their own homes and want this government, through mortgage interest deductibility and other means, to help them. These people want the Government of Canada to adopt that kind of policy because it indicates that it is prepared to back up with its policy those Canadians who want to go out and build for themselves.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Talk about the cost.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I shall talk about the cost, and I will talk about the consequences as well.
November 20, 1978

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In real figures.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I shall talk about the cost in real figures too. I am sure the parliamentary secretary is aware, and I know he is doing his job as a parliamentary secretary and as a partisan, that the two industries which would be most dramatically affected by my policy would be the house building industry, which is almost 100 per cent Canadian-owned. We would not only be helping young, older and middle aged Canadians who want to build homes, we would also be stimulating a highly productive part of the Canadian economy. We would be creating jobs for Canadians and growth for Canada, which in turn would provide revenue for the Government of Canada and the governments of the provinces. It would provide the kind of stimulus which is singularly absent in the budget brought down by this government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
All members are proud of the constituencies they come from and I am sure they think they cannot be matched by any other constituency in the country. I had the opportunity to be home in my riding on the weekend, to meet some of the people who work and live in the constituency of Rocky Mountain which stretches along the western mountains and foothills of Alberta. These are people who work harder than we do in this House of Commons, people who go down in coal mines every day, who work outside in winter, and who run farm operations which require them to keep the schedule that calves keep when they are being born, a schedule much less predictable than you, sir, can enforce in this House of Commons. They are hard working Canadians who have their counterparts in every constituency in this country.
One of my privileges as national leader is to have the opportunity to travel this country, to go to Newfoundland and visit the little community of Trepassey and see people who go out every day in violent seas to fish for food, and to travel across this country and see people who want to build.
Many of these people came to this country because they knew that there was opportunity to build, and that is the nature of this country. What we need is a national policy, including an economic policy, that is in keeping with the building nature of this country, rather than in conflict. For a decade we have had a government which has not trusted the people of Canada, and it is evident again in the budget. Instead of allowing private entrepreneurs to acquire businesses which could be best operated in the private sector, the government moves in and buys. Instead of helping young Canadians and other Canadians who want to go out and build their homes, the government says no. Instead, this government goes out to younger Canadians and Canadians on low incomes and says: "You are too rich. How do we, those of us sitting in Outremont, know you are too rich? Because you want to own a home." That is what the Prime Minister said, and that is why he opposed our policy.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Oh, oh!
The Budget-Mr. D. J. Johnston

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I will not get into that matter, Mr. Speaker, because it is a subject for another debate, but it certainly indicates an attitude toward Canadians. There is here, in this party, a determination to establish a government which will introduce policies which will encourage the building instinct of ordinary Canadians. It will be a refreshing change and we look forward to introducing such policies as soon as we can after the next election.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
These are my first remarks in this House, Mr. Speaker. Indeed, it is a great honour and privilege for a number of reasons. First of all, simply being an elected representative of the Canadian people is a great honour, as is representing the riding of Westmount, which, as hon. members know, will soon be redesignated as Saint Henri-Westmount. It is an unexpected pleasure to have the opportunity to listen to and follow the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), and accordingly I would like to depart from some of the general comments which I intended to make at the outset about my riding-which I understand are traditional and to which I will come back in due course-to comment briefly upon some of the statements made by the Leader of the Opposition with regard to the budget.
I have sometimes been a critic of budgets in the past, but I must say that I am proud, as a humble backbencher, to be associated, however indirectly, with the budget handed down last week.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have to assume that the Leader of the Opposition, because he really did not address himself to any of the substantive issues contained in the budget, must be in agreement, by and large, with the proposals contained in it.
I learned some things in the course of my campaign. I am a neophyte and a debutante with no political experience, and, in the course of my campaign, my Conservative adversary, who was a very able adversary, let it be known to me that he had been at a candidate's school. This was my first criticism of my own party, because I did not have the benefit of candidate school. It appeared to me during the course of the campaign and after listening to a number of members of the opposition, including its leader, that candidate school specializes in a particular form of humour, a good deal of gloom and doom, and the preaching of a lot of platitudes.
The comments which I intend to make to this House today will be less humorous, with less doom and gloom, and I hope that there will not be too many platitudes. However, I would like to point out that the Leader of the Opposition did make one statement which I share wholeheartedly with him, and that is, that this is not a country beset by problems, but a country of unlimited opportunity. I was delighted to hear the Leader of the Opposition make that statement, because it has long been my impression during the course of the last several years and, in my election campaign that too much gloom and

November 20, 1978
The Budget-Mr. D. J. Johnston
doom is being preached in this country, not only by the opposition but from other quarters as well.
I see this country today as a country of unlimited potential and energy, with enormous coal reserves, untapped riches in the tar sands, hydroelectric power which could double within the next 15 years, and with one of the great forest reserves of the world, unmatched by any nation except, as I understand it, Russia and Brazil. We are endowed with one of the great freshwater reservoirs, minerals, and twice as much farmland per capita as the United States, although we are not quite as productive. Canada is a country of unlimited opportunity. That is why I say, that I am delighted to see those opportunities married to responsible financial policies, such as those contained in the budget brought down by the government.
It is clear to even the most cynical observer that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), in his budget rejected seductive political proposals in favour of long-term economic growth which the country requires.
Turning for a moment to my own riding, I should like to point out that indeed it is not only an honour and privilege to represent Westmount, but also a challenge. I am called upon to fill the vacancy created by the resignation of the Hon. "Bud" Drury, whose distinguished career as a soldier, public servant and politician is well known to members on both sides of the House.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I was delighted to hear the hon. Leader of the Opposition pay homage to Mr. Drury. Even in his retirement from the House, he has gone on to accept several difficult mandates, and still serves the Canadian people.
In its wisdom, the riding of Westmount selected a Liberal by an overwhelming majority in the recent by-elections. Yet, I feel that in the minds of many Canadians, the Westmount riding conjures up the image of one of the two solitudes about which Hugh MacLennan wrote so many years ago: the solitude of the affluent English in the province of Quebec. The riding of Westmount is not such a bastion or fortress of the English-speaking population of the province of Quebec. In fact, Westmount today is symbolic of the Canada of the future, the pluralistic society which brings together so many of the wonderful differences present in Canada, such as racial, religious, economic and social. All those differences are present in that great riding. The riding comprises one of the most important influential Jewish communities in Canada, as well as one of the most important business communities and universities, combining all that in a riding which is predominantly English and very substantially bilingual.
From time to time the premier of Quebec, Mr. Rene Levesque, has made reference to the metaphor used by Sir Winston Churchill of two scorpions in a bottle being representative of the relationship between the French and the English. I can assure Your Honour and all members of the

House, that if that metaphor is applicable anywhere is Canada-and I personally do not think it is-certainly it is not applicable in my riding or in the city of Montreal.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In fact, Mr. Speaker, the Westmount riding represents the Canada of tomorrow, where learning and speaking both official languages will be considered an opportunity and not an obligation.
At present, Mr. Speaker, we are observing in the West-mount riding a profound change in the attitude of the Englishspeaking population which is willingly taking part in the francization of Quebec. Anglophones, for example, are seeking opportunities to communicate and speak French with their fellow citizens, and it is astonishing to see, Mr. Speaker, that most of my Anglophone friends' children are attending either French schools or French immersion schools where both languages are taught. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, despite the Parti Quebecois' efforts to create an attitude of confrontation between Anglophones and Francophones, exactly the opposite is happening today.
Mr. Speaker, since the conquest, Canadian history has taught us that the division between French and English in the province of Quebec is based on religious rather than language differences. Up until now these religious differences have almost separated the two societies or prevented their integration. In my view, the ease with which English-speaking Irish Catholics have integrated themselves into the French community, for example, is proof of this theory. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that is why today we Find Francophones with names like Burns, O'Neill and Johnson, even in the Parti Quebecois.
As we know, Mr. Speaker, these religious barriers have nearly disappeared. This is a very great change in Quebec. In my opinion, relations have never been as friendly and as positive. I believe that far from being confirmed, these two solitudes, of which Hugh MacLellan wrote, are rapidly getting closer together. We, English-speaking Canadians, who have not the slightest intention of leaving the province of Quebec, see in all this the potential for a multicultural society.
